claims.text: The initial as-cast Mg–Fe–Al–Cr–Ti HEA is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state.
Isothermal annealing at 500 °C initiates decomposition of the metastable alloy.
The first transformation stage is spinodal decomposition into Mg-enriched and Mg-depleted nanodomains.
Mg-enriched and Mg-depleted nanodomains form within approximately 10 h at 500 °C.
The second transformation stage is nucleation and growth of ordered L12-type intermetallic precipitates.
Ordered L12-type precipitates develop by 100 h of annealing at 500 °C.
The proposed transformation is diffusion-controlled and proceeds from Mg-rich domain formation to subsequent atomic ordering into L12 phases.
Annealing produces a fine intragranular network of nanoscale intermetallic precipitates.
The nanoscale precipitate network impedes oxygen and ion diffusion.
Impeded oxygen and ion diffusion retains or improves high-temperature oxidation and aqueous corrosion resistance relative to the as-cast state.
After annealing for 100 h at 500 °C, oxidation mass gain during a 500 °C, 100 h oxidation test will be approximately 20–40% lower than for the as-cast baseline.
After annealing for 100 h at 500 °C, corrosion potential in 3.5 wt% NaCl will be approximately 50 mV nobler than for the as-cast baseline.
The proposed behavior is valid for service and heat-treatment temperatures from 300 °C to 600 °C and durations up to approximately 100 h.
A precipitate volume fraction not exceeding 10% after 100 h at 500 °C would falsify the proposed L12-mediated mechanism.
Oxidation mass gain within ±5% of the as-cast baseline, together with a corrosion-potential shift below 20 mV, would falsify the predicted resistance improvement.
